title: Silk Route homestays: what to expect at each stop
meta_description: What Old Silk Route homestays are really like in 2026: rooms, toilets, heating, food, rates of ₹1,200–2,500 per person and which village suits whom.
summary: Almost every bed on the Old Silk Route is in a family homestay. Expect a clean, simple room, thick quilts, home-cooked dinner and breakfast, and rates of about ₹1,200–1,800 per person a night, or ₹2,000–2,500 for newer rooms with attached bathrooms. Heating and hot water are limited, especially at Nathang.

sections.heading: Why the Silk Route is a homestay route
paras: There are no hotels in the usual sense between Lingtam and Kupup. The villages along the road are small: Zuluk has a few hundred residents and Nathang far fewer, and land in an Army area is not something an outside investor can buy and build on. What grew instead, over the last fifteen years or so, is a network of family homestays. A household adds two or three rooms, sometimes a new floor, and takes in travellers who arrive with their driver in the afternoon and leave after breakfast.

This is the best thing about the route. You eat what the family eats, warm your hands by their kitchen stove, and hear about yak herding, BRO road work and the last big snow from people who live with them. It also means you should arrive with homestay expectations, not hotel ones. Rooms are clean and beds are warm, but the plumbing, power and heating depend on altitude and the season.

sections.heading: Rooms, toilets and warmth
paras: A typical Silk Route room has two or three beds with heavy cotton quilts or blankets, a small table, hooks for clothes and a single bulb. Newer rooms, especially at Zuluk and Padamchen, have wooden floors, attached bathrooms with western toilets and a geyser that works when the power does. Older or higher homes may share a bathroom across the corridor, and at Nathang water can freeze in pipes from December, so hot water comes by the bucket.

Heating is the main thing to ask about. Some homes offer an electric room heater for about ₹200–300 a night, which only works when voltage allows. Others rely on the kitchen stove and extra quilts. Bring thermal inner wear, a warm cap and socks to sleep in from October to March, and a hot-water bottle if you feel the cold. Power cuts are common, so carry a torch and a power bank.
list: Usually provided: bed, quilts, towels on request, drinking water, dinner and breakfast
Sometimes provided: attached bathroom, geyser, room heater, Wi-Fi
Rarely provided: reliable mobile data above Zuluk, room service, menu choice
Bring: torch, power bank, slippers, thermals, small towel, refillable bottle

sections.heading: A day in a Silk Route homestay
paras: Most travellers reach their homestay between two and four in the afternoon, after the permit stop at Rongli and the climb through the forest. The family will usually have tea ready, and the first hour is for settling in: finding the bathroom, switching on the geyser if there is one, and putting on a warmer layer as the light goes. Above Zuluk the temperature falls fast after sunset, and by six it is cold enough that everyone drifts towards the kitchen.

Dinner is early, often by seven or half past, because the family's day starts before dawn. Expect to be in bed by nine. If you are going up to Thambi or Lungthung for sunrise, your driver will knock at around four thirty and your host may send you off with a flask of tea. You come back to a hot breakfast, pack, settle the bill in cash, and are on the road by eight or nine. It is a simple rhythm, and most people find that one or two nights of it is the part of the trip they talk about afterwards.

sections.heading: The food
paras: Homestay food on the Silk Route is simple and generous. Dinner is usually rice, dal, a seasonal vegetable, often a meat or egg curry, pickle and sometimes a local green such as squash shoots or nettle. Breakfast is puri or paratha with potato, bread and omelette, or noodles, with sweet milk tea. Many homes serve evening tea with pakoras or Maggi when you arrive cold from the road.

Tell the family your preferences when you arrive, not at the dinner table. Vegetarian and Jain meals are possible if they know in time, and most homes will make the food less spicy for children. Lunch is not always included on travel days; you will eat at Rongli, a tea stall at Thambi or Kupup, or carry something packed from breakfast. Alcohol is the family's call; ask before you open a bottle in the house.

At Nathang and Kupup you may be offered yak products: churpi, the hard dried cheese that herders chew for hours, and sometimes yak butter in salted tea. Try them once. Fresh vegetables are scarcer the higher you go, especially in winter, when much of the food is carried up from Rongli, so do not expect a salad at 4,000 m.

sections.heading: Which village suits whom
paras: Each overnight stop on the route has a slightly different character, and choosing well matters more for comfort and acclimatisation than choosing a particular house.

Our usual pattern is a low first night at Padamchen, Lingtam, Rolep or Aritar, a second night at Zuluk, and an optional third at Nathang for fit adults. Families with young children do better with two nights at Zuluk and Nathang by day. Photographers who want sunrise without a pre-dawn drive pick Lungthung. In each village quality varies more between houses than between villages, so it pays to book through someone who has slept there recently and can tell you which rooms have attached bathrooms, which families cook best and which houses stay warm.

sections.heading: Sleeping high: Nathang and acclimatisation
paras: Nathang, at about 4,000 m, is the highest place most travellers sleep in Sikkim outside North Sikkim's Thangu. A night there is a fine experience, with the plateau silent under stars, but it is also where most Silk Route headaches and sleepless nights happen. Our rule is simple: do not sleep at Nathang on the night you arrive in the hills. Spend at least one night lower, at Padamchen, Zuluk or Aritar, then go up.

At Nathang drink plenty of water, skip alcohol, eat a light dinner and keep warm. Mild headache and poor sleep are common. Vomiting, confusion, breathlessness at rest or a headache that pain relievers do not touch are warning signs: tell your host and driver and go down that night, because descent is the treatment. Families with young children, older travellers and anyone with heart or lung conditions are better off sleeping at Zuluk and visiting Nathang by day.

sections.heading: Booking, paying and being a good guest
paras: Most Silk Route homestays are booked through drivers, agents or by phone, and only some appear on booking sites. Booking through us or your driver usually gets the standard rate and the permit handled in the same message. Pay in cash where you can; UPI works only where there is signal.
A homestay is someone's home. A few habits make the stay better for everyone.
list: Ask before photographing family members, the prayer room or the kitchen.
Take off your shoes where the family does.
Keep noise down after 9 pm; the family starts early and so do the yaks.
Use water carefully, especially in winter, when it is carried or heated by hand.
Carry your plastic and batteries back down; waste disposal is hard at this height.
If something is wrong, tell your host quietly and early; most problems are fixed in minutes.

faqs.a: No, not in the usual sense. Zuluk has family homestays, some with newer rooms, attached bathrooms and geysers, at about ₹1,300–2,500 per person a night with dinner and breakfast. For a hotel room, sleep at Aritar or Gangtok and visit by day, accepting a long drive. Book ahead in October, November and late December.

faqs.q: Do Silk Route homestays have attached bathrooms?
faqs.a: Many newer rooms at Zuluk and Padamchen do, with western toilets and a geyser that works when the power does. Older homes and some at Nathang share a bathroom, and in deep winter water may come by the bucket because pipes freeze. Ask for an attached bathroom when you book; it usually costs ₹300–700 more per person.

faqs.q: Is food included in Silk Route homestays?
faqs.a: Dinner and breakfast are almost always included, and many homes add evening tea with a snack. Lunch is often not included on travel days. Expect rice, dal, vegetables, often an egg or meat curry, and puri or paratha for breakfast. Tell your host in advance if you need vegetarian, Jain or less spicy food.

faqs.q: Is it safe to stay overnight at Nathang?
faqs.a: For healthy adults who have spent a night lower first, yes. Nathang is about 4,000 m, so headache and poor sleep are common. Do not sleep there on your first night in the hills. Drink water, skip alcohol and keep warm. If anyone has vomiting, confusion or breathlessness at rest, go down at once. Young children are better off at Zuluk.

faqs.q: Do homestays on the Silk Route have heating?
faqs.a: Some offer an electric room heater for about ₹200–300 a night, which depends on the voltage. Many rely on thick quilts and a warm kitchen stove. From October to March bring thermals, a warm cap and socks to sleep in. At Nathang nights fall well below freezing from November, and to around −10 °C or lower in January.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Zuluk?
faqs.a: Patchy. Some networks work in and around Zuluk, often weakly, and coverage becomes poor or absent around Thambi, Nathang and Kupup. Some homestays have Wi-Fi that works when power and the link allow. Tell family you may be out of reach for a day, and download maps and tickets before you leave Rongli.

faqs.q: Which is better for a night: Padamchen or Zuluk?
faqs.a: Zuluk if you want to be close to the loops and Thambi sunrise and are fit and acclimatised; it has the most homestays. Padamchen if you are travelling with children or older parents, arriving late, or want a gentler first night at about 2,200 m. Many of our trips use Padamchen first, then Zuluk or Nathang.

faqs.q: How do I book a Silk Route homestay?
faqs.a: Most are booked by phone through drivers, agents or the families themselves; only some are on booking sites. Booking through us or your driver usually gets the standard rate and the permit processed at the same time. Book two to four weeks ahead for October, November and late December. Pay the balance in cash.

faqs.q: Can foreigners stay in Silk Route homestays?
faqs.a: Not at Padamchen, Zuluk, Lungthung, Nathang or Kupup, which are inside the protected area closed to foreign nationals. Foreigners can stay at homestays and hotels in Aritar, Rhenock and Pakyong town, which are outside it; for Rolep, ask us. Check current status before you travel, as permit rules in border areas change.
